claim: In the 1998 Delhi Assembly election (70 seats) Congress (INC) won 52 seats and the BJP won 15.

evidence.locator: Part I, Performance of Political Parties (report p.7), BJP row

method: Read ECI statistical report PDF, extracted text; columns are CONTESTED, WON, FD, VOTES, %, % in seats contested.
notes: BJP contested 67 seats, INC 70. Others in the same table: JD won 1; List of Successful Candidates shows 2 Independents (Badarpur, Seelampur). 52+15+1+2=70.

claim: 1998 vote shares in Delhi: INC 47.76%, BJP 34.02% of valid votes polled (BJP 35.82% in the seats it contested).

evidence.locator: Performance of Political Parties, BJP row

method: As C-C01.
notes: Dar et al. say 'just 34 percent' (consistent).

claim: Before: in the 1993 Delhi Assembly election the BJP won 49 of 70 seats with 42.82% of votes; Congress won 14 with 34.48%.

evidence.locator: Performance of Political Parties, BJP row

method: Read ECI 1993 report.
notes: Swing 1993->1998: BJP 49->15 seats, 42.82%->34.02% votes; INC 14->52 seats, 34.48%->47.76%. Also JD fell from 4 seats to 1.

evidence.quote: iii. POLLING PERCENTAGE                            50.89%                    46.41%             48.99%
iii. POLLING PERCENTAGE                            64.56%                     58.27%             61.75%

method: ECI Highlights page.
notes: Turnout fell by about 13 points while the BJP vote fell by 8.8 points in share: a fact the film can use with care (do not infer cause).

claim: Poll date was 25 November 1998 (result 28 Nov).
method: The ECI statistical report (12 pages, text searched for 'date', 'Nov') carries no poll date. Only a search-engine summary of Wikipedia gave 25 Nov 1998.
notes: Need ECI press note / Delhi CEO / Gazette notification. Do not state the date until read at a primary.

claim: Dar, Gupta & Verma find a 'political price cycle' in onion prices and not in the other 15 commodities tested.

evidence.quote: ‘political price cycle’ in onions and not in other commodities, confirming a commonly
held (but hitherto empirically untested) view that onion prices are an electorally salient issue.

method: Read the PDF abstract.
notes: Abstract in full: 'Do prices of essential food commodities vary with the timing of elections? Using weekly retail price data of 16 food items between 1993 and 2012 in 28 cities across India, we find existence of a political price cycle in onions and not in other commodities...' Version read is dated 5 October 2018 (working paper; I did not find a journal version).

claim: Data: weekly retail (and wholesale) prices of 16 food items, 28 urban centres in 18 states, 1993-2012, collected by the Price Monitoring Cell, Department of Consumer Affairs, Government of India.

evidence.quote: These prices have been collected by the Price Monitoring Cell (PMC) of the de-
ties from 1993 to 2012. This data is available for twenty-eight urban centres spread across eighteen

method: Read section 3.
notes: Authors say they matched 37 newspaper (Times of India) prices to check the PMC data. Delhi is one of the 28 centres.

claim: Direction of the finding: onion retail prices tend to DROP as a state election approaches and RISE in the early part of the incumbent's term (a cycle in timing).

evidence.quote: coefficients indicate the retail prices of onions tend to drop as elections approach and rise during the

method: Read results section; Table 2 coefficients on weeks-to-election 0.006661** etc.
notes: WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM: it does not claim onion prices decide elections or caused any defeat; it tests whether prices are lower near elections. The authors call the mechanism (incumbent-trader collusion) 'suggestive' and the cycle 'strongest' under three conditions, listed in the abstract as 'suggestive evidence'. Not specific to 1998 or to Delhi. State-assembly elections only (variation in state election timing).

claim: Dar et al's explanation: onion trade is concentrated; one market, Lasalgaon, accounts for a significant share of trade.

evidence.quote: the hands of few traders differentiates onions from other commodities (a single market, Lasalgaon

method: Read intro.
notes: This is the authors' hypothesis, supported by CCI and NCAER reports they cite, not shown as a measured fact in this paper. 'Largest onion market in India' is stated in the data note (see C-C20).

claim: The 1998 narrative: Dar et al say the BJP won all 7 Delhi Lok Sabha seats in March 1998 with 51.7% votes, then lost the assembly election months later, and that 'most accounts' attribute the defeat to onion prices which they say doubled over a few months (citing Dugger, NYT, Oct 1998).

evidence.quote: the party’s vote share declined sharply in Delhi to just 34 percent. Most accounts of the election
used daily in most households doubled over a few months, voters decided to punish the incumbent

method: Read the paper's background paragraph; the cited NYT piece (Dugger 1998) not opened.
notes: The 34% matches ECI (C-C02). The 'doubled' figure and 'most accounts' are the authors' summary of press, not a measured price series. The Lok Sabha 7/7 and 51.7% are not checked against ECI Lok Sabha 1998 report (other agent / TODO). Paper's own wording: 'partly due to a spike in vegetable prices' (line 476). Treat 'onions caused the loss' as DISPUTED-by-nuance: onions are one named factor in press accounts.

claim: After the 1998 crisis the central government brought onions under the Essential Commodities Act; removed in October 2004.

evidence.quote: after the onion-crisis of 1998, the central government brought onions within the purview of the

method: Paper's statement; no gazette notification opened.
notes: Needs the MoCA/Consumer Affairs notification (other agent or lead). Paper says they were re-added later when the BJP returned (text lines 543-546).

claim: August 1998: Union commerce minister Ramakrishna Hegde directed a temporary export ban on onions; said imports would be considered if prices stayed high.

evidence.quote: Union commerce minister Ramakrishna Hegde has directed the commerce secretary to impose a temporary ban on the export of onions
Importing onions is one of the steps being considered, Hegde said.

method: Read period newspaper (P3). DGFT notification and Lok Sabha answer not reachable (see BLOCKED).
notes: 'Directed ... to impose' is a direction, not the gazetted ban. A January 1998 ban is mentioned only inside the Shiv Sena memorandum.

claim: Price figures reported in Aug 1998: a Shiv Sena memorandum said a ban in January 1998 cut onions 'from Rs 25 per kg to Rs 8-10 per kg'; it blamed heat before harvest, the Gujarat cyclone and floods, and alleged 2 lakh tonnes hoarded in Nashik district.

evidence.quote: a similar ban on export of onions had been imposed in January this year which resulted in a price reduction from Rs 25 per kg to Rs 8-10 per kg
nearly 1.5 lakh tonnes of onion had been exported

method: Period newspaper reporting a party memorandum.
notes: INTERESTED PARTY (Shiv Sena, wanting an export ban). Do NOT use as an official price. No Delhi retail Rs/kg series for Oct-Nov 1998 found at a primary. Government causes (Rajya Sabha 9 Jul 1998 / Lok Sabha) not read: BLOCKED.

claim: NAFED sold onions at subsidised prices in Delhi, Chennai and Hyderabad in Jan-Feb 1998 (1,777 tonnes, 2 Jan-21 Feb 1998).
method: Only a web-search summary of Rajya Sabha unstarred question 184, 9 Jul 1998 (rsdebate.nic.in/.../PQ_184_09071998_U2448_p59_p60.pdf). The site now returns an app shell, not the PDF.
notes: BLOCKED: read in a browser at sansad.in / eparlib. Also unread: LS 23 Feb 1999 answer on imports (10,000 t authorised, NAFED imported 687 t; export ban partly lifted 21.1.99) at eparlib.sansad.in/bitstream/123456789/798601/1/12_IV_23021999_p102_p102_79.pdf.

claim: Sattvic texts/tradition class onions and garlic as rajasic (stimulating), to be avoided in a sattvic diet.

evidence.locator: Journal of Ethnic Foods review, food classification para
evidence.quote: Rajasic foods like meat, eggs, fish, spices, onions, garlic, hot peppers and pickles confer emotional, passionate, restless qualities

method: Read PMC full text.
notes: Review citing 'literature'; classification traced to Gita 17.7 by the authors, but the Gita verse itself does not name onion (not checked by me; flag).

claim: Sri Vedanta Desika's Ahara Niyama lists garlic and onions among over-stimulating foods forbidden.

evidence.quote: foods that over-stimulate (such as garlic, onions, radish, drumsticks, varieties of guards, greens, and mushrooms) cause an imbalance between the mind and body are forbidden from consumption

method: Review's paraphrase of the text.
notes: Reason given: over-stimulation / imbalance of mind and body. The Sanskrit text itself not read. Journal of Hindu Studies Srirangam paper not found.

claim: A Sri Vaishnava institution's guidance: even reducing onion and garlic is 'not ok'; food habits must change.

evidence.quote: Ex: onion and garlic. It won’t be ok. We have to change our food habits.

method: Community page; the community says.
notes: Shows the rule is held by specific communities (Sri Vaishnava, Udupi/Puri temples per search snippets, unread). NOT evidence that all Hindus avoid onion.

claim: Jain practice: lay Jains avoid onion in varying degrees; the reason given is the unnecessary death of the whole plant and disruption of many jivas; monks and nuns avoid the whole list.

evidence.quote: Most lay Jains do not avoid all of the above
since they involve the unnecessary death of the whole plant and the disruption of many Jivas
Monks and nuns, however, must take great care to avoid every item on the list.

method: Read page. Anantakaya ('infinite bodies') is item 43 in the page's list of 44.
notes: No scholarly edition (Tattvartha Sutra commentary, Flugel 2003 Terapanth) retrieved: UPGRADE NEEDED. Page says 'Many Jains are also keen to avoid ... anything which is grown underground (such as potatoes, carrots, onions, etc.)': i.e. varies by person.

claim: Not all Hindus avoid onion; practice varies by community and household.

evidence.quote: In rural India, even in the absence of other food, people

method: No peer-reviewed survey of onion-avoidance among Hindus found. Dar footnote 12 says rural people eat rotis with raw onions and chillies.
notes: Journal of Hindu Studies / Srirangam article not located; need an NFHS-style or ethnographic source. A statement such as 'a share of Hindus avoid it' needs a number: none found.

claim: Lasalgaon (Nashik) is the largest onion market in India.

evidence.quote: The largest market for onions in India is Lasalgaon, Maharashtra.

method: Authors' statement (no source given there). 'Asia's biggest' appears only in news pages; no APMC/NHRDF/Ministry statement opened.
notes: Verdict on myth 'Lasalgaon is Asia's biggest': Unverifiable at a primary. Safer: 'the largest in India, per Dar et al.', still to confirm with APMC volume data.

claim: Charaka Samhita (Sutrasthana 27.175) describes the onion (palandu): promotes kapha, treats vata but not pitta, a good adjuvant for food, strengthening, heavy, aphrodisiac, appetizing.

evidence.quote: The onion is promotive of Kapha, curative of Vata but not of Pitta; it is a good adjuvant for food and is strengthening, heavy, aphrodisiac and appetizing.
The onion/palandu (Allium cepa Linn) promotes kapha

method: Read translation of an Ayurvedic scholarly society (1949) and a verse viewer.
notes: Shows onion is an ancient medicinal/food item in the text. I did not establish a date for the text; do not date it in the film without a scholarly source. (Onion is treated as a food 'adjuvant', not as forbidden.)

claim: Allium cepa remains at Raja-Nal-Ka-Tila (Belan valley, UP) from the Early Iron Age, dated about 1300-700 BCE.
method: Could not open: search summaries say Pokharia 2008 (The Palaeobotanist, jpsonline.co.in) tabulates Allium cepa at Raja-Nal-Ka-Tila (Saraswat 2002; Saraswat & Pokharia 2003b) with 1600-700 BC, while Spengler et al 2020 (Veg Hist Archaeobot, doi 10.1007/s00334-020-00798-8, Barikot) lists the site as 1300-700 BCE. jpsonline.co.in did not resolve (NXDOMAIN), Springer redirected to login.
notes: DISPUTED dates (1600 vs 1300 BCE start) as reported by snippets; neither read by me. Single site, single phase. Do not say 'onions have been grown in India for X years' from this. Needs Saraswat & Pokharia 2003 (Pragdhara or Man & Environment) or the report on the Raja-Nal-ka-Tila excavation.

claim: Myth: 'Onions toppled governments in 1980 and 1998'. In 1980 Indira Gandhi made onion prices an election cry; in 1998 the BJP lost Delhi.

evidence.quote: the pyaaz (onion) elections as onion prices were an overwhelming concern for voters.
party took out front page newspaper ads blaming the incumbent Charan Singh government for fail-
Onion price rise in 1980 helped Indira Gandhi to topple India’s first non-Congress government.

method: Dar et al summarise Wallace 1980, Auerbach (Washington Post 9 Jan 1980: prices fell ~20% before Gandhi took office). Period newspapers/Lok Sabha 1979-80 debates not opened.
notes: 1980: Congress campaigned on onion prices (Dar et al); 'toppled' is embellished: the election followed the fall of the Charan Singh government (as the paper says he was the incumbent), onion was a campaign theme, not shown to be the cause. 1998: a STATE government (Delhi) lost; BJP's central government stayed. Dar says 'partly'. Verdict: Embellished. Corrected wording: 'Onion prices were a central campaign issue in 1980 and are widely cited, alongside other factors, in the BJP's 1998 loss in Delhi (assembly seats 49 to 15).'

claim: Myth: India is the largest onion exporter.

evidence.quote: India is the world’s second largest producer of onions

method: Dar fn 12 (citing Chengappa 2012, now dated) says India is 2nd largest PRODUCER and a net exporter. Search snippets from APEDA/PIB (unread) rank the Netherlands first and India second by export quantity; another APEDA table puts India first by production (~28.65%).
notes: Hand to the trade/production agents with UN Comtrade (HS 070310) and FAOSTAT. Do not say 'largest exporter' from my work.
